@Meng Wu has covered this very thoroughly. Let me add one thing: assuming the calculation is done correctly, in which case do you get 3 dB?


Defining sound pressure level

First, take a sound signal in the time domain that varies over time, p(t)[1]

Its sound pressure level is strictly defined as

L=20log10(prms/p0)[dB]

where prms is the root mean square of the sound pressure over the stretch of signal being evaluated, calculated like this:

prms=1T∫0Tp2(t)dt

Broadly speaking, the sound pressure level represents the average magnitude of p(t).


But when we listen, what we hear is a signal that changes over time. Say the average sound pressure level in a concert hall over one minute is 60 dB: the individual instruments still rise and fall within that minute, and they aren’t at 60 dB the whole time.


So when we think about what we actually hear, we also have to consider the time-varying signal itself as it reaches the ear.


“Adding up” sounds

Suppose we have two signals whose RMS sound pressures over the same time interval are p1 and p2, and both have the same sound pressure level, 90 dB.

There are three cases worth considering[2]:

in phase, in antiphase and incoherent.

See the figure below.


  1. In phase, the two waveforms are identical. If, as the asker suggests, two pianos play at the same time, the sound pressure level at the ear goes up by 6 dB. But that +6 dB rests on a lot of assumptions: both pianos are the same distance from the ear, they’re tuned identically, the direct and reflected sound of the fundamentals and harmonics take the same paths, binaural effects are left out, and so on;

2. The extreme case (very unlikely in practice): if the two signals are exactly opposite in phase, they interfere destructively at the ear and we hear nothing at all (as @Markus Sheng pointed out). This is why we need to treat the signal as time-varying, not just as an averaged sound pressure level. Active noise cancellation works on exactly this principle.

3. Setting the original question aside, if the two signals are incoherent, the term p1p2 in Lsum can be neglected, and the result becomes +3 dB. Now back to point 1: why did we need all those assumptions? Because in reality the signals reaching the ear may well have become incoherent.


I’ve answered a question before about how we perceive pitch, if you’re interested:

How do we perceive how high or low a sound is?
